newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Mexico battles agains U.S. corn sweeteners.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mexico battles agains U.S. corn sweeteners.

text.p: In the battle to quench the thirst of Mexican consumers, U.S. forces carry corn syrup, the defenders lob sugar and victory may be decided by the World Trade Organization.

Mexico -- at least demographically -- is a young, thirsty nation. Not only is more than half of its population under the age of 21, but its per capita soft drink consumption is second only to the United States.
Both factors make it an attractive market for U.S. high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) producers such as Cargill Inc., A.E. Staley Manufacturing Co., CPC International Inc. and Archer Daniels Midland Co.

Fifteen years ago, those companies became dominant in the U.S. soft drink sweetener market. Now Mexican sugar producers, who sell about 35 percent of their sugar to Mexican soft drink bottlers, fear they will be the next to fall.
After U.S. exports of HFCS to Mexico surged to 194,800 tonnes in 1996, Mexico sugar producers complained to their government.
TARIFFS IMPOSED IN JUNE
The message was heard and in late June, Mexico imposed new HFCS import tariffs that were four to five times the levels applied before the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The tariffs also varied widely, based on the difference between prices charged by individual U.S. exporters for HFCS and Mexican domestic sugar prices in 1996.
Mexico levied the steepest tariffs for grade 55 HFCS, which is used to make soft drinks, on CPC International at $175.50 per tonne, and the lowest tariffs on Cargill at $63.42.

There was also a wide tariff range for grade 42 HFCS used in baking and to make jams, jellies and candy. A.E. Staley and CPC International were at the top with tariffs of $125.30 per tonne, and Cargill was again at the bottom at $66.57.

In response to the Mexican action, both the U.S. House and Senate passed resolutions urging the U.S. Trade Representative's Office to look into the case and determine if there were grounds for a WTO challenge.
That matter is still under review. But in July, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky expressed U.S. concerns to Mexico's top trade official, a USTR spokeswoman said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department forecasts that 530 million bushels of corn will go into HFCS production in 1997/98 (Sep-Aug), more than triple the level of the early 1980s.
Corn sweeteners, which also include glucose and dextrose, now account for more than half of U.S. sweetener consumption, compared to less than 20 percent in 1975.
DISPUTE UNITES MEXICAN SUGAR INDUSTRY
Mexican sugar producers argued that cheap HFCS imports from the United States unfairly threaten their industry.
In Mexico, the HFCS threat has united mill owners, sugar cane growers and the mill workers' union, three main industry forces that are normally at loggerheads.

"It could mean between 20,000-25,000 lost jobs," Enrique Ramos, secretary general of the 70,000-strong National Sugar Industry Workers' Union, told reporters recently. "Maybe 25 mill closures have also been talked about," he added. Mexico currently has 61 active mills.

Mexico's sugar industry is very labor intensive, with the mill owners and the sugar union powerful forces in a sensitive sector for the government. Only about four percent of the national harvest is cut by machines, the rest by hand. Most sugar cane growers are also small landowners.
Whether the Mexican government's finding can stand up to a WTO challenge turns on several points, according to U.S. industry experts.
Chuck Conner, president of U.S. Corn Refiners Association, acknowledged that U.S. manufacturers can sell HFCS for as much as 50 percent less than the price of Mexican refined sugar.
However, that price gap is similiar to the one that exists in the United States and reflects technological differences in production, among other factors, he said.
"It's like comparing the compact disc to an old 45 record," Conner said.
OWNERSHIP, LEGAL STANDING ISSUES

But even with more efficient production, it would be hard for U.S. HFCS manufacturers to capture all of the Mexican soft drink market because of the co-ownership of some Mexican bottling facility and sugar mills, he said.
The corn refiners also argue that the Mexican sugar industry does not have proper legal "standing" to file an anti-dumping case against HFCS.
About 100,000 tonnes of HFCS was produced in Mexico in 1996, so any complaint about dumping should come from that sector instead of the sugar industry, Conner said.
Mexican sugar producers argue they have standing because HFCS and sugar are similar products.
The corn refiners counter this point by noting that HFCS and sugar are processed from different raw materials and have different chemical compositions.
Also, "there are a number of uses for sugar that HFCS cannot replace," Conner said.
The next step is an "expert disposition" hearing next week in Mexico. That will give both sides an opportunity to present outside witnesses to bolster their case.
U.S. exporters do not expect the hearing to prompt Mexico to reduce its tariffs, but it could set the stage for a successful WTO challenge further down the road, Conner said.
